title: Sale of Nigeria's state power company (NEPA/PHCN)
point: Abuja, where the Bureau of Public Enterprises ran the sale and the Abuja distribution company was handed over (national measure)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Its Privatization Support Project (IDA credit, US$114.29 million, approved June 2001, closed December 2009) paid advisers to break up NEPA into separate companies, design the new power market, study tariffs, and prepare and run the sale of the generation and distribution companies. The World Bank says the October 2010 Roadmap for Power Sector Reform called for carrying out the privatization agenda developed with this project's support.

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: In its September 2007 letter of intent for the fourth review under the Policy Support Instrument, the government set completing the bid opening for concessioning the Transmission Company of Nigeria as a step before the final IMF Board meeting.

conditions: World Bank Privatization Support Project power components: corporate restructuring of NEPA, 'privatization of entities formed from NEPA', and a tariff strategy study (World Bank completion report, 2011). IMF Policy Support Instrument: the government committed to 'complete bid opening for concessioning of Transmission Company of Nigeria' before the final IMF Board meeting (Nigeria letter of intent, 26 September 2007).

companies.name: KANN Consortium
companies.role: Took over the Abuja Electricity Distribution Company at the November 2013 handover (Daily Trust).

companies.name: Manitoba Hydro International
companies.role: Given managerial control of the Transmission Company of Nigeria (Daily Trust). Head office in Winnipeg per Devex.

community: On 1 November 2013 ten distribution and four generation companies passed to private owners. Daily Trust reported that the new owners disengaged electricity staff immediately after the handover. The electricity workers' union NUEE said more than 50,000 former PHCN staff were still owed entitlements and over 5,000 had received nothing (Guardian Nigeria). In December 2019 the union said over 2,000 disengaged staff had not been paid since 2013, that the new distribution companies paid some workers half salaries, and that some did not pass on deducted pension contributions (TheCable). A new tariff order (MYTO 2) in June 2013 raised electricity bills (Daily Trust).
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: The handover took place amid NUEE strikes over unpaid severance; an agreement signed in late October 2013 set payment before the end of November (Daily Trust). In December 2019 the union struck again over unpaid benefits, causing hours of blackouts, and called it off in less than 24 hours after federal government intervention (TheCable). Transmission stayed in state hands under a management contract.

title: Sale of Eleme Petrochemicals
point: Eleme petrochemical plant near Port Harcourt (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Its completion report for the Privatization Support Project lists the Eleme sale (US$225 million, 11.9% of all proceeds) among privatizations achieved to date under the programme the project supported. Its private arm, the IFC, lent US$75 million and mobilised US$80 million from commercial lenders for the purchase (Bretton Woods Project).

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: The Bretton Woods Project says the sale of the Eleme plant was a structural reform of the IMF Policy Support Instrument in October 2005.

conditions: The World Bank Privatization Support Project (2001-2009) financed the privatization programme under which Eleme was sold (World Bank completion report, 2011). The Bretton Woods Project (2008) says the Eleme sale was a structural reform under the IMF Policy Support Instrument in October 2005.

companies.name: Indorama Group
companies.role: Buyer, through its Nigerian subsidiary, for about US$225 million; Bretton Woods Project calls it an Indonesian firm and says it was given a 75% stake although a memorandum had set a 51/49 split.

community: The National Union of Petroleum and Natural Gas Workers said the price was 'not worth the spare parts available at the plant'. The Bretton Woods Project reports that, after a government committee assessed staffing needs, staff fell from 1,000 to 296.
suppression: The Bretton Woods Project cites informal reports that troops took the plant by force after the state oil company NNPC refused to hand it over.
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: Indorama's Nigerian subsidiary bought the plant for about US$225 million (Bretton Woods Project; World Bank completion report).

title: Sale of Ghana's state gold mines at Tarkwa
point: Tarkwa gold mine, Wassa West District (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Its Mining Sector Rehabilitation Project (IDA credit 1921-GH, approved June 1988) paid to rehabilitate and restructure the State Gold Mining Corporation (SGMC) and to attract investors. The World Bank says the credit facilitated the sale of SGMC's three mines, including Tarkwa. It also helped draft regulations to implement the 1986 Minerals and Mining Law.

conditions: Under the Mining Sector Rehabilitation Project, the government and lenders agreed to fund the work needed to attract investors and sell all of SGMC's mines, with cost cutting and downsizing at SGMC (World Bank completion report, 1997).

companies.name: Gold Fields
companies.role: Has managed the Tarkwa mine since July 1993 (World Bank completion report).

community: Earthworks reports that mining displaced 30,000 people in the Wassa area between 1990 and 1998 (it does not say who counted). It says farmland was taken 'often using force and without adequate compensation'. On 16 October 2001 a tailings dam burst at the Tarkwa mine run by Gold Fields Ghana, leaving more than 1,000 people without drinking water and affecting at least five villages. Researcher William Tsuma (2010) says the general shift from underground to surface mining made community displacement a regular occurrence.
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: SGMC was virtually dissolved by the end of March 1997, with liquidation under way. Tarkwa output rose from 20,528 ounces (1989) to 47,450 ounces (1996). The World Bank rated the project highly satisfactory. The village of Abekoase reached an out-of-court settlement with the mining company in December 2003 (Earthworks).

title: Hungary 1998 pension privatization

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Granted a one-tranche Public Sector Adjustment Loan (PSAL) of US$150 million. Its policy matrix, the conditions for Board presentation, included adopting a new multi-pillar system with a mandatory private pillar and tightening public pension terms. An earlier US$132 million loan (1993) funded pension and health insurance administration.

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: The ILO says the IMF and World Bank recommended pension privatization and soon dominated the reform debate.

conditions: PSAL policy actions: 'New multi-pillar system adopted', mandatory for new labour-force entrants; retirement age raised from 55 (women) and 60 (men) to 62; indexation changed from net wages to a mixed wage/price formula; private fund rules acceptable to the World Bank (World Bank IEG Hungary evaluation, 2007).
community: Pensions in the privatized system were estimated to be 9.8-12.5% lower than before for people with 20 years of contributions and over 18% lower with 30 years. Coverage fell from about 75% of the labour force before 1998 to 71.8% (2009). Administrative costs were above 10% of contributions, reaching up to 14.5% in some cases. Transition costs rose from 0.3% of GDP in 1998 to 1.2% in 2010 (ILO, 2018).
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: Act CI of October 2010 moved private pension savings back to the state system. The government used 243 billion forints of the transferred assets to repay an IMF loan. The IMF, World Bank, EU and OECD criticized the reversal (ILO, 2018).

sources.title: Hungary - Pension reform and the development of pension systems: an evaluation of World Bank assistance
Reversing Pension Privatizations: Rebuilding public pension systems in Eastern Europe and Latin America
sources.publisher: International Labour Organization (Ortiz, Durán-Valverde, Urban, Wodsak, eds.)

confidence_note: Parliament passed the pension laws in 1996-1997; the World Bank evaluation says the PSAL conditions were to be met before the loan was granted.
check_note: Corrected the fee figure to 'above 10%, up to 14.5% in some cases' as the ILO states, and described the 1993 loan as funding pension and health administration rather than the reform.

title: Serbia 2015 state firm bankruptcies under IMF programme
point: Belgrade, seat of the Privatization Agency (firms were spread across Serbia)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Stand-By Arrangement of SDR 935.4 million (about €1.2 billion) approved 23 February 2015. The IMF press release lists reducing state aid to state-owned enterprises and says about 500 of them were in a first group set for resolution or privatization.

conditions: IMF Press Release 15/67: the programme includes reducing state aid to state-owned enterprises, with about 500 in a first group for resolution or privatization. The government adopted an action plan to start bankruptcy of 188 companies on 31 January 2015 (Government of Serbia).
community: Reuters reported about 5,000 job losses from the planned bankruptcy of the 188 firms. By mid-2016, about 300 firms employing about 25,000 workers had been liquidated, merged or sold. Five firms declared 'strategic', including Zastava vozila in Kragujevac, went bankrupt. The Heinrich Böll Foundation found no record of large severance payments in the budget.
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: About 250 firms with about 55,000 workers were still unresolved in July 2016, and 11 strategic firms with about 21,000 workers remained (Heinrich Böll Foundation).

title: Ukraine 2015 coal subsidy cut and miners' unpaid wages
point: Novovolynsk state coal mines, site of 2016 hunger strike (protests also in Kyiv)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Extended Fund Facility put to the IMF Board on 11 March 2015. The programme's 2015 budget eliminated subsidies to the coal-mining industry and cut subsidies to state firms, including coal, by 1.1% of GDP (IMF Country Report 15/69). The Kyiv Post describes the subsidy cut pledge as 'a stipulation' of the 2015 IMF loan programme.

conditions: IMF Country Report 15/69: the 2015 budget 'eliminates subsidies that supported the inefficient coal-mining industry' (worth 0.6% of GDP in 2014).
community: On 28 January 2015 about 1,500 miners picketed the Cabinet of Ministers in Kyiv. Wage arrears stood at UAH 600 million (US$38 million), with some unpaid since August 2014. The union warned over 50,000 jobs were at risk (IndustriALL). In 2016 a state plan aimed to support only about a third of 35 state mines, close or sell the rest and cut about 10,000 jobs (20%). Miners were owed three months' pay (Kyiv Post).
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: On 7 November 2016, 50 workers at the No. 10 Novovolynska mine began a hunger strike; 300 people from the same mine also blocked the Yahodyn checkpoint on the Polish border. The energy minister promised all wage debts would be paid by January. The 2017 budget set coal support at UAH 1.8 billion, against the union's demand of UAH 4.6 billion (Kyiv Post).

title: Senegal 2023 fuel and electricity price rise
point: Dakar, capital (approximate); fare rises were also reported in Bignona

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Raising energy prices was a prior action (a step required before the IMF board meeting) in the January 2023 review of Senegal's Stand-By Arrangement, Standby Credit Facility and Policy Coordination Instrument (IMF Country Report 23/30).

conditions: IMF Country Report 23/30 lists as a prior action: 'Raise energy prices to limit electricity and fuel subsidies' to 2.7% of GDP in 2023, with protection for vulnerable households. Publishing a roadmap to gradually eliminate energy subsidies was also a prior action. Without action, subsidies would have been about 4.2% of GDP in 2023.
community: From January 2023 electricity rose by 18.97 CFA francs per kWh for low-voltage users and 22.79 for medium-voltage users, and diesel and premium fuel by 100 CFA francs per litre (Enerdata). Seneweb reported a shared-taxi ride in Bignona going from 500 to 1,000 CFA francs, and said bakers, carpenters, tailors and hairdressers faced the new power prices. The urban transport association Aftu announced fare rises.
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: The transport minister said no fare rise had been agreed and that direct support for operators was being discussed; a transport strike was set for Tuesday 17 January (Seneweb, 16 January 2023). The government expected to save about 258 billion CFA francs and aimed to end energy subsidies by 2025 (Enerdata). The IMF board completed the reviews on 9 January 2023.

title: Brazil 1999 IMF program social spending cuts
point: Brasília, where protesters gathered outside the World Bank office (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Three-year stand-by credit of SDR 13 billion (about US$18.1 billion) approved 2 December 1998, with primary surplus targets and spending cuts (IMF press release 98/59).

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: The World Bank President said he was ready to recommend up to US$4.5 billion in support of Brazil's programme (IMF press release 98/59). In 1999 the World Bank also suspended disbursements of approved loans to Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul, states in dispute with the federal government over debt repayments (Bretton Woods Project).

conditions: Primary surpluses of 2.6% of GDP in 1999, 2.8% in 2000 and 3% in 2001, with 'substantial cuts in discretionary current and capital spending', a higher financial transactions tax and higher social security contributions by public employees; budget savings of about 3.4% of GDP in 1999 (IMF press release 98/59).
community: Social Watch Brazil reports the social area lost R$2.04 billion (23.7%) in 1999 and 25 of 31 trade union-financed programmes for low-income people ended. The Bretton Woods Project reports the 1999 land reform budget was cut 42.6% and social action in sanitation 73% from 1998, and a rural settlements programme was scrapped. Unemployment in Greater São Paulo reached a record 19.3% in 1999 (DIEESE/SEADE, cited by Social Watch).
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: NGOs, unions, students and opposition parties protested outside the World Bank office in Brasília (Bretton Woods Project, March 1999). Brazil exceeded the IMF surplus target; Social Watch notes a R$30 billion primary surplus (to September 1999) was absorbed by R$85 billion of federal debt interest.
